newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico April industrial figure eases jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico April industrial figure eases jitters.

text.p: Mexico's industrial production grew much faster than expected during April, easing worries after a weak March number stirred fears the nascent recovery was running out of gas.
Industrial activity in April grew 15 percent compared with the same month of the year before, fueled mostly by a 16.3 percent leap in manufacturing and a 15.4 percent jump in construction.
"It's good news. There is no reason to think the economy is going gangbusters, but it is a positive figure," said Carlos Rosales, chief economist at Bancomer bank in Mexico City.
Mexico's stock market welcomed the news, driving up stock prices about half a percent to 4,277 points on the key IPC index in late trade.

A Reuters survey of 13 Mexican banks and brokerages had forecast industrial production of 7.92 percent during April. Rosales at Bancomer and Vector brokerage were the closest at 12.40 and 12.50 percent, respectively.
A major factor accounting for the unusual jump in industrial production was statistical distortion owing to timing of Easter, economists said.
Since the Easter holiday week fell in March this year and April last year, the number of working days in each month was not comparable to the previous year's month.
Because of the statistical difference, March's 4.2 percent growth in industrial activity fell well short of expectations and April's 15 percent figure was well above.
"A lot of economists failed to take into account the full effect of the difference in working days," Rosales said. "After this month, things should return to normal."
Boosted government spending ahead of July's mid-term elections also drove industrial production upwards, economists said.

The average of the March and April industrial output compared to the same period of the year earlier shows about 9.5 percent growth in industrial activity, according to Sergio Martin, economist at ING Barings in Mexico City.
"That figure is overall above expectations," he said.
Martin said he was leery of interpreting the April figure as a sign the economy would continue to grow at this pace for the rest of the year.
"We are in pre-election time. The April figure could be contaminated by a greater government spending ahead of the elections that has helped the economy," he said.
Government spending is visible in the money market, where the central bank has reined in some liquidity in order to neutralize the greater government outlay, he said.

Martin said the faster pace of industrial activity would probably force him to raise his second quarter GDP estimate of 3.7 percent. Rosales said he was comfortable with his 6.9 percent second quarter GDP estimate.
Rosales added that second quarter GDP would look artificially strong because it was being compared to a weak period of 1996.
"The rest of the year should look more normal. The growth rates will look more homogenous," he said.
